description: Single-pane health view of the OAK DMS stack. The top row answers 'is the system healthy?'; every row below it answers 'what is causing the problem?'.

panels.description: Is the host metrics agent (node-exporter) reporting? DOWN means we are blind to the server's CPU, memory and disk - the host itself may still be fine, but nothing in the 'CPU & memory' or 'Disk & storage' rows can be trusted. Investigate if it stays DOWN for more than a couple of minutes.
panels.title: System Health

panels.description: Is the DMS backend (dms-core) answering its metrics endpoint? DOWN means the application is not responding and users are almost certainly seeing errors. This is the first thing to check whenever the system 'feels broken'.
panels.title: Backend

panels.description: Can PostgreSQL be reached? DOWN means the database is unreachable or refusing connections - uploads, logins and search will all fail. Treat any sustained DOWN as a production outage.
panels.title: Database

panels.description: Can Redis be reached? DOWN means caching and session state are unavailable: the system usually keeps working but gets noticeably slower and logs cache errors. Worry if it does not recover within a few minutes.
panels.title: Redis

panels.description: Is the RabbitMQ broker up? DOWN means background work - scanning, OCR and workflow messages - stops being delivered. Nothing is lost, but jobs queue up and the backlog panels at the bottom of this dashboard will start climbing.
panels.title: RabbitMQ

panels.description: Free space left on the tightest real filesystem on the server. Below 15% is a warning - plan a cleanup or add disk. Below 5% is urgent: document uploads and the database can fail outright once the disk fills.
panels.title: Storage free

panels.description: How many documents are currently sitting in the OCR 'failed' state. Zero is the healthy value. A handful usually means a few unreadable scans; more than 20 points at a broken OCR worker or a bad batch import and should be investigated.
panels.title: OCR failures

panels.description: Total CPU used on the server, averaged over all cores. Short spikes during imports or OCR runs are normal. Sustained time above 80% means the machine itself is the bottleneck - expect slow page loads and growing queues.
panels.title: Host CPU %

panels.description: Share of the server's RAM that is not available to new work. Above 85% for a sustained period risks swapping or the kernel killing containers - use the container memory panels to see which service is growing.
panels.title: Host memory %

panels.description: Java heap the backend is actually using, against the ceiling it is allowed. A sawtooth pattern is healthy garbage collection. Worry when 'used' climbs steadily towards 'max' and never falls back - that is a memory leak and it ends in an OutOfMemoryError.
panels.title: JVM heap used vs max

panels.description: How hard the backend process is working and how many threads it is running. Threads climbing without a matching rise in traffic usually means requests are blocked on something slow (database, storage or an external call) and threads are piling up waiting for it.
panels.title: JVM CPU & threads

panels.description: Seconds per second that the backend spends paused for garbage collection. Near zero is healthy. Above 0.1 (a tenth of wall-clock time) the application is stalling regularly and users will feel it - usually a sign the heap is too small or leaking.
panels.title: GC pause rate

panels.description: How full each mounted filesystem is. Watch the line that is climbing, not the highest one: a mount heading for 85% deserves attention now, and anything over 95% can stop uploads and crash PostgreSQL.
panels.title: Disk usage % per mount

panels.description: Bytes per second read from and written to disk. Heavy sustained writes during an import are expected; constant high I/O when nobody is uploading suggests the database is churning or something is logging excessively, and it will show up as slow API responses.
panels.title: Disk I/O

panels.description: Network traffic in and out of the server on real interfaces. Useful for confirming that a slow system is actually busy serving documents rather than stuck, and for spotting a transfer that is saturating the link.
panels.title: Network throughput

panels.description: Total size of all document content DMS is holding in its storage area. Compare its growth rate against the free space above to estimate how long the current disk will last.
panels.title: DMS stored bytes

panels.description: Total number of documents held in the system. This should only ever go up during normal operation - a sudden drop means documents were deleted or purged, which is worth confirming was intentional.
panels.title: Documents stored

panels.description: How long the server has been running since its last boot. A value that resets to near zero means the machine rebooted - if that was not planned, check for a crash or a host-level failure before trusting anything else on this dashboard.
panels.title: System uptime

panels.description: Requests per second handled by the backend, stacked by HTTP status class. 2xx is normal traffic; a growing band of 4xx suggests clients sending bad requests, and any visible 5xx band means the server is failing requests outright.
panels.title: Request rate by status

panels.description: Percentage of requests the backend answered with a server error. Under 1% is background noise. Above 1% something is genuinely broken; above 5% users are being blocked and this should be treated as an incident.
panels.title: Error rate %

panels.description: How long requests take: half are faster than p50, 95% are faster than p95. Judge the system by p95 - if it climbs while p50 stays flat, a subset of requests (usually large uploads or heavy searches) is suffering. Everything rising together points at the database or the host.
panels.title: Response time p50 / p95 / p99

panels.description: The ten slowest API endpoints right now, by 95th-percentile response time. When the system feels sluggish this names the specific screen or operation to blame. Anything consistently over a second or two is worth a look.
panels.title: Slowest endpoints (p95)

panels.description: Open PostgreSQL connections against the configured maximum. If the two lines converge, new connections start being refused and the application will fail with connection errors - either something is leaking connections or the pool needs resizing.
panels.title: DB connections vs max

panels.description: The backend's own database connection pool. Idle connections are healthy spare capacity. 'Pending' above zero means requests are queueing for a connection - that directly becomes slow API responses, and it is the clearest sign the pool is undersized or queries are too slow.
panels.title: Hikari connection pool

panels.description: Database transactions committed and rolled back per second. A steady commit rate is normal work. A rising rollback rate means transactions are failing - usually application errors, deadlocks or constraint violations - and is worth correlating with the API error rate above.
panels.title: Transaction rate

panels.description: On-disk size of each database. Steady growth is expected as documents are added; a sudden jump usually means a bulk import, and growth that never flattens should be checked against the free disk space in the row above.
panels.title: Database size

panels.description: CPU used by each container in the stack, as a percentage of one core. Use this to attribute high host CPU to a specific service - one container sitting at several hundred percent is usually the cause of a slow system.
panels.title: Container CPU

panels.description: Memory actively held by each container. A line that only ever climbs is a leak and will eventually be killed by the kernel; a sawtooth is normal. Compare against the 'memory vs limit' panel to see how much headroom is left.
panels.title: Container memory

panels.description: How close each container is to its configured memory limit (only containers that have one appear here). Above 75% is worth watching; above 90% the container is close to being killed and restarted, which shows up as a blip in the restart panel.
panels.title: Memory vs limit %

panels.description: Inbound network traffic per container. Useful for seeing which service is doing the talking during a busy period, and for spotting a container that has gone silent while the rest of the stack is still active.
panels.title: Container network in

panels.description: How many times each container started in the last hour. Zero everywhere is what you want. Anything above zero outside a planned deployment means a container crashed and was restarted - check that service's memory and logs.
panels.title: Container restarts (last hour)

panels.description: Memory Redis is using for cached data and sessions. Flat or gently rising is normal. If it climbs towards the container's memory limit, Redis will start evicting keys and the hit rate next to this panel will fall.
panels.title: Redis memory

panels.description: Share of cache lookups that found what they were looking for. Above 90% means the cache is doing its job. A sharp drop means Redis was restarted, is evicting data, or the application is asking for things that were never cached - expect more database load and slower responses.
panels.title: Redis hit rate %

panels.description: Commands Redis is handling per second - a simple measure of how busy the cache is. It should roughly track user activity; a flatline at zero while the backend is up suggests the application has stopped talking to Redis.
panels.title: Redis ops/sec

panels.description: Messages waiting to be picked up (ready) and messages handed to a worker but not yet finished (unacked). Both should stay low and flat. A steadily rising 'ready' line means work is arriving faster than it is being processed, or the consumers have stopped.
panels.title: RabbitMQ messages ready / unacked

panels.description: How many clients are currently connected to Redis. A number that climbs without ever falling back points at connections being leaked by the application and will eventually exhaust Redis.
panels.title: Redis connections

panels.description: Number of workers currently subscribed to RabbitMQ queues. If this drops to zero while messages are waiting, nothing is processing background work - scanning and OCR will silently stop until a consumer reconnects.
panels.title: RabbitMQ consumers

panels.description: How many queues exist on the broker. This is normally a fixed number; an unexpected change means queues were declared or removed by a deployment or configuration change.
panels.title: RabbitMQ queue count

panels.description: How many documents are entering the system each second, split by how they arrived. This is the business pulse of DMS: a drop to zero during working hours means uploads or imports have stopped working, even if every service above still shows UP.
panels.title: Documents ingested per second

panels.description: Ingestion attempts per second, stacked by how they ended. A healthy system is almost entirely successes. A growing band of failures or rejections means uploads are being refused - typically virus scanning, an unsupported file type or storage problems.
panels.title: Scan outcomes per second

panels.description: Time taken to ingest a document, for the slowest 5% of them. Rising p95 with unchanged volume means scanning is getting slower - check virus scanning, storage I/O and the OCR backlog before users start reporting timeouts.
panels.title: Scan duration p95

panels.description: Documents waiting in each scanning state. A small, fluctuating backlog is normal. A line that only climbs means work is arriving faster than it is being processed, or a worker has stopped - check the RabbitMQ consumers panel above.
panels.title: Scan backlog

panels.description: Current count of documents in each OCR state. 'Completed' should dominate. A large 'pending' or 'processing' figure that does not shrink means OCR is stalled; any growth in 'failed' means documents are being left without searchable text.
panels.title: OCR documents by status

panels.description: Rate of workflow tasks being approved, rejected or otherwise decided. This shows whether people are actually working through their queues. A flatline during office hours usually means the workflow UI or its backing service is broken rather than that nobody is working.
panels.title: Workflow decisions

title: OAK DMS System Monitoring
